subject: Biology
title: The Great Barrier Reef
description: A 60-second lesson on The Great Barrier Reef.

hook.text: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on Earth—visible from space.

buildup.text: Stretching 2,300 km along Australia's coast, it contains over 2,900 individual reef systems.

discovery.text: It's home to 1,500 fish species, 400 coral species, and 4,000 types of mollusk.

twist.text: Mass bleaching events have killed up to 50% of its coral in recent decades due to warming seas.

climax.text: The reef generates $6.4 billion annually for Australia through tourism and fishing.

punchline.text: The biggest living thing on Earth is dying in plain sight.

quiz.question: How long is the Great Barrier Reef?

details.summary: The Great Barrier Reef stretches over 2,300 kilometers along Australia's northeast coast and is the largest living structure on Earth, visible from space. Composed of nearly 3,000 individual reef systems, it supports over 1,500 fish species and 400 types of coral.
details.whyItMatters: The Great Barrier Reef is Earth's most iconic marine ecosystem and a barometer of ocean health. Its repeated mass bleaching events since 2016 warn that even the world's best-managed reefs cannot withstand unchecked global warming.
takeaways: The reef stretches 2,300 kilometers and contains nearly 3,000 reef systems
It has experienced six mass bleaching events since 1998 with increasing severity
The reef supports a $6.4 billion tourism industry and over 60,000 jobs

faq.question: How badly has the Great Barrier Reef been damaged?
faq.answer: Over 90 percent of the reef has been bleached at least once. The 2016 and 2017 back-to-back events killed approximately half the coral in the northern section. While some recovery occurs between events, the increasing frequency leaves less time for healing.

faq.question: Can the Great Barrier Reef be saved?
faq.answer: Researchers are developing heat-tolerant coral strains, improving water quality management, and controlling crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks. However, the reef's long-term survival depends primarily on reducing global carbon emissions to limit ocean warming.
